My scopeAligned production, inspection, retest, scrap, and defect definitions, then coordinated improvement schedules and retest results.Used MSA results to separate judgement errors from real defects, then checked jig tolerance, recipe, consumables, vision, and inspection conditions one factor at a time.Verified result / current stageMeasured result · TeamEffective good yield in the reviewed scope: about 40%→98.7%Verified output · IndividualReflected confirmed conditions in SOP, QCP, P-FMEA, inspection criteria, and training materialTeam boundaryYield was a cross-functional team result. My role as assembly process lead was to align criteria, priorities, and revalidation.
Disclosure scope: Company source data and customer specifications are confidential, so this case is anonymized and limited to career records and work I directly performed.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered Good-product yield on the 2170 assembly line was initially about 40%. Changing equipment conditions from that headline number alone could mistake a judgment error for a real defect. The reverse was equally risky: treating an actual process defect as an inspection issue would allow it to recur. Before changing the process, the production, inspection, retest, and scrap quantities needed one yield denominator.
My scope As the assembly-process lead, I organized the production plan, WIP, defects, and downtime. I aligned the denominator and defect names used by production, quality, equipment, and development, coordinated the MSA review and condition-by-condition retests, and carried confirmed conditions into field standards.
Workflow Align the yield denominator → separate judgment error from actual defects with MSA → check jigs, recipes, consumables, and inspection conditions → retest one condition at a time → update SOP, QCP, and P-FMEA
Key decisions and verification I used MSA to review operator judgment error and measurement-system variation before classifying actual process defects. Jigs, recipes, consumable wear, and inspection conditions were checked as one system, but only one condition changed in each trial. The test item, inspection method, and decision rule stayed fixed. A condition entered the line baseline only after repeat results supported it. Result and standardization The team result recorded in career material was an improvement in good-product yield from about 40% to 98.7%. Confirmed conditions and checks were added to SOPs, QCP, P-FMEA, inspection criteria, and operator training. The practical standard was that different operators and shifts would calculate and judge yield on the same basis.
Transferability When yield is low, verify the denominator and the measurement system before tuning a recipe. Then separate equipment, consumable, and inspection variables and retest one condition at a time so the cause and effect remain explainable.
Limits The 98.7% figure is a career result for this line, verification period, and denominator, not a public-data recalculation or a universal result for every 2170 line. Company drawings, recipes, raw quality records, and customer specifications remain confidential.
Links and evidence Public linksPublic material for reviewing project evidence and the live user surface.
There is no separate public GitHub repository or report. Quantitative results are described from career records.
In an interview I can explain how the denominator was aligned, how MSA separated judgment error, the sequence of retests, and the scope of the standard-work updates.

Useful learning requires more than showing many questions: answers must remain hidden before submission, and evidence must explain why an answer is right or wrong afterward.Live · Selected material remains deferredPeriod / basisLast completed validation snapshot · Jul 30, 2026Project formPersonal AI use · Evidence-based learning platformProblem to solveQuestion, answer, explanation, source, and rights status were mixed, so automatically publishing weakly supported material risked incorrect learning and rights issues.
My scopeDesigned and validated the select→submit→evidence→mistake-review flow, publication decisions, and answer non-disclosure before submission.Verified result / current stageVerified output · IndividualAnswer non-disclosure before submission and evidence-led mistake review after submissionCurrent stage · IndividualLive, with weakly supported or rights-unclear material kept out of publicationTeam boundaryAI assists classification, drafting, and checks; a person decides source, rights, answer conflicts, and publication.
Disclosure scope: Only the public live surface and last completed validation scope are described; work in progress is excluded from achievements.
The case follows the learner's actual path from question selection through mistake review.
Problem Maintenance-qualification material fragments questions, answers, theory, NCS units, and practical visuals across sources. A fluent AI explanation can still teach the wrong thing when answer candidates conflict or image rights are unclear. A learning flow also fails if the answer or explanation is already present in the client response before submission, even when the screen hides it.
The project did not start with a question-volume target. It publishes only material with verified answer, source, and rights evidence. Anything missing one of those elements keeps the same ID and an explicit reason while staying out of the public set.
Representative user scene A learner selects a CBT question, chooses an answer, and submits it. Before submission, the learner receives no answer, explanation, or option-level feedback. After submission, the learner sees the answer and explanation together with the linked source and theory evidence. A wrong option becomes a path back through that evidence for mistake-based learning.
Written-response and practical material follow the same evidence rules without being forced into one answer format. A question or visual without sufficient publication support stays out of the learning path with its deferral reason preserved.
What a first-time visitor sees The top navigation mirrors the learning sequence. A learner starts with Theory, moves to the Written mock exam, practices constructed answers in the written-response areas, and uses Practical information to review pneumatic, hydraulic, welding, preparation, and test-center differences. Search is the entry point for returning to a specific concept or question.
Written mock start screenThe screen offers an 80-question four-subject mock, random practice, and custom configuration. Answers and explanations are not sent before submission.

Surface What a newcomer does Rule behind the surface Theory and search Find a concept and its connected evidence Only approved lessons and sources are visible Written mock Choose a full, random, or custom session No duplicate question in a session; no answer before submission Written-response study and mock Practice keywords and answer order Constructed-answer structure stays separate from multiple choice Practical information Review pneumatic, hydraulic, welding, preparation, and center differences Official public tasks and rights-cleared material take priority Review Revisit the wrong choice and linked theory Answers, explanations, and option feedback appear only after submission What the tool does—and does not do The tool connects question selection, submission, evidence review, and mistake learning. Each question carries a stable ID, assessment type, answer state, theory link, source, rights state, publication decision, and deferral reason. Publication eligibility means the answer, source, and rights have all been checked; it does not merely mean that content exists.
The tool does not replace official exam material or guarantee a passing outcome. It does not publish an explanation merely because AI finds it plausible. Answer conflicts remain held_answer_conflict; missing visual evidence or unclear rights remain held_asset_missing.
Data, AI, and human roles The data keeps evidence and review state beside the question. Question, theory, NCS evidence, answer state, rights, and publication status share a stable identity so later evidence can be added without erasing the history of uncertainty.
AI assisted with classification, duplicate and semantic-mismatch candidates, explanation and option-feedback drafts, and regression-check ideas. A human reviewed original sources, actual answers, conflicts, image and drawing rights, publication decisions, and final deployment approval. AI plausibility is not publication evidence.
Screen, data, and repository structure The learner surface is only the last layer. Source material does not flow straight into a page. It is structured, assigned a publication state, and transformed into a learner-safe response. The submission API can verify an answer, but the pre-submit response excludes the answer, explanation, and option feedback.
Import and generation steps turn source material and review notes into stable IDs and structured records. Content repositories read each question together with theory, source, rights, and review state. A publication filter separates published, in-review, and held material. App Router pages and APIs receive only the public DTO needed for theory, practice, submission, and review. Unit, integration, and browser tests check the data contract, answer leakage, and representative learner flows. There is no separate public Git repository. The following is a disclosure-safe responsibility map; it does not expose private source files or credentials.
src/app/ pages, learner routes, and submission APIs src/components/ question cards, tabs, progress, and review UI src/lib/content/ question/theory repositories and publication decisions src/lib/security/ pre-submit answer-leak protection scripts/ source import, generation, verification, and packaging tests/ unit, integration, and browser user flows supabase/ account, review-role, and data policies A repository reader should start with src/app to see entry routes, move to src/lib/content to understand what reaches the screen, and then inspect src/lib/security and tests for the publication and no-answer-leak contracts.
Build sequence Inventory source material and reviewed notes, then assign stable IDs. Separate CBT, written-response, and practical types and connect questions to theory, NCS evidence, and sources. Review answer conflicts and visual rights, keeping incomplete material out of publication. Use Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Zod, and Tailwind to build the select→submit→evidence→mistake-learning flow. Exclude answers, explanations, and option feedback from pre-submit responses; check the data and representative flow with Vitest and Playwright/Chromium. Read back the static artifact through Cloudflare Pages and Sites. Current result The last completed snapshot is dated 30 July 2026 on Node.js 24.14.0.

Company value and limitations The same approach can support company training or maintenance-knowledge systems. Keeping source, revision state, rights, and human review beside work knowledge makes AI-generated explanations easier to distinguish from approved training content. Connecting question selection to evidence review and mistake learning also turns a document collection into a designed learning behavior.
The limits remain visible. Material without answer or rights evidence is still deferred, and full-E2E residuals remain. Official source material takes priority when it differs from the site. In-progress skill changes and an unimplemented inventory contract are excluded from this result.

Yield and delivery were team results.
Disclosure scope: Equipment drawings, customer specifications, and raw measurements remain confidential; only the verified acceptance process and my scope are described.
The sequence below generalizes the actual work within a publicly shareable scope.
The three-minute case Why it mattered An automatic cycle on one machine does not make a pilot line production-ready. Interfaces and acceptance criteria must work across the line, and unmet items must be retested against the same criteria after supplier action. The task was to manage 13 detailed processes and 11 core systems as one acceptance flow.
My scope My scope covered acceptance criteria and FAT/SAT sheets, Punch List tracking, supplier actions and retest review, and daily 200-cell production operation. I connected equipment action status with material, WIP, and work priorities. Yield and delivery metrics are identified separately as team results.
Workflow Define acceptance criteria → FAT/SAT → Punch List → supplier action → retest → daily 200-cell operation
Key decisions and verification Acceptance criteria were defined before testing so the supplier and site team judged the same items. A Punch List item was not closed on a planned action alone. I tracked the supplier action through a retest against the same criterion. Production planning did not sit outside equipment acceptance. The daily 200-cell operation checked whether material, WIP, and work flow held together after FAT/SAT. Result and standardization The team recorded at least 95% pilot assembly yield and 100% delivery compliance. Acceptance criteria, Punch List and retest results, work standards, and production-history rules were connected so equipment acceptance led into daily operation on one baseline.
Transferability Equipment acceptance is not a one-time FAT or SAT event. A line is ready only when acceptance criteria, open items, supplier actions, retests, and actual production operation remain traceable as one chain.
Limits The yield and delivery figures are team results from pilot production, not long-term mass-production performance or a claim about each machine in isolation. Company acceptance records, equipment drawings, recipes, and customer specifications remain confidential.
Links and evidence Public linksPublic material for reviewing project evidence and the live user surface.
There is no separate public GitHub repository or report. Process capability (Cpk) and the measurement system (Gage R&R) are presented as separate checks.
In an interview I can explain how the acceptance criteria were set, how Punch List items stayed open through retest, and how the work transitioned into daily 200-cell operation.

Unemployment-benefit questions are safer when categorized and linked to official and individual verification paths rather than answered with a simple eligibility verdict.Live · Policies may changePeriod / basisPublic validation snapshot · Jul 19, 2026Project formPersonal AI use · Official-source Q&AProblem to solveSimilar questions can have different answers depending on separation reason, insured period, and individual notices, so general guidance must not replace administrative decisions.
My scopeGrouped 165 anonymized questions into eight types and connected official sources, practical guides, and static-page generation.Verified result / current stageMeasured result · Individual165 anonymized questions classified into eight typesCurrent stage · IndividualStatic Q&A and guide linked to official sources are liveTeam boundaryAI assists classification and drafting; a person verifies sources, legal wording, and final publication.
Disclosure scope: Original conversations and personal notices are not published; only anonymized question types and official-source links are used.
The case follows how a user finds a question type and moves to an official verification path.
Problem A short question such as “Can I receive unemployment benefit after resigning?” may depend on separation reason, insured periods, documents, job-search activity, and agency review. A one-sentence eligibility decision can conflict with current policy or the actual administrative disposition. Publishing the source conversations would also expose personal context and repeat many similar questions.
The project is not an eligibility chatbot. It is a static information service that guides de-identified questions toward official confirmation paths.
Representative user scene A person who has left a job selects the type closest to their situation. The guide identifies facts to check first—such as separation reason, insured period, documents, and job-search activity—then links to the relevant Work24, Ministry of Employment and Labor, and statute sources. The user confirms the final position through an individual agency notice, current Work24 guidance, and the competent employment center rather than relying on the site’s wording.
No raw chat, name, contact information, employer, or case detail appears on the site.
What a first-time visitor sees The home page does not start with a chatbot prompt. It first shows what the visitor should check today, then offers eight situation categories and links to practical guides. This keeps a person from treating one generated sentence as an eligibility decision.
Home: decide what to check before searching for an answerThe public home page places the next official confirmation step before the question catalogue. The displayed counts describe the published snapshot, not an eligibility result.

Selecting a guide opens a sequence of facts, documents, and official channels to confirm. A visitor can therefore understand both the next action and the limit of the guide without knowing the data model behind it.

Users can return to the same evidence and caveats instead of receiving an unconstrained free-form answer.
The tool does not decide individual eligibility, payment, or appeal outcomes. It does not submit applications or access a Work24 account. It is not automatically current after a policy change. Individual notices, Work24, and the competent employment center always take priority over the site.
Data, AI, and human roles The data separates question type, situation, facts and documents to check, official source, and caveat. Q&A, guides, search pages, and structured data come from one source rather than separately maintained copies.
AI assisted with taxonomy drafts, duplicate and search clusters, answer structures, and metadata. A human de-identified the source questions, checked Work24, Ministry of Employment and Labor, and statute links, and reviewed wording that could be read as an individual decision.

Mixing in execution authority can also lead to an unapproved external change.
My scopeDesigned the flow that selects relevant ontology and LLM-wiki knowledge, composes agent roles, tools, evidence, outputs, and stop conditions, and checks approval and result read-back around external changes.Verified result / current stageVerified output · IndividualAI agent composition and execution platform that binds roles, tools, evidence, and stop conditions to ontology and LLM-wiki knowledgeCurrent stage · IndividualAgent composition, local execution foundation, and safety layer verified · not connected to productionTeam boundaryAI assists request classification, knowledge retrieval, agent-definition drafts, and result summaries. People decide knowledge standards, tool boundaries, and approval for external changes.
Disclosure scope: The public case covers agent composition, local execution, and the last completed safety-layer validation; internal ontology/wiki content, repositories, environments, and authority details remain private.
The article generalizes how ontology and wiki knowledge is selected to compose and run an agent through a practical work example.
What this platform is Approval gates are not the product by themselves. This project is an AI agent platform that uses knowledge, terminology, and operating rules from an ontology and an LLM wiki to compose and run an agent for a requested task.
The ontology connects related concepts such as equipment, processes, documents, and roles. The LLM wiki provides task guidance, operating sequences, tool instructions, and cautions. The platform selects the relevant knowledge and assembles an executable agent definition containing its role, tools, evidence sources, output format, and stop conditions.
Authority, approval, and evidence checks are the platform’s safety layer. The ability to generate an answer does not automatically permit an agent to submit an order, deploy a change, or modify access. Evidence and human approval are checked separately before an external effect is allowed.
Why I built it When an agent is defined only through a long prompt, terminology can be interpreted inconsistently and the same rules must be repeated for every project. Source documents and tool boundaries also become mixed into the conversation. As the number of agents grows, knowledge and operating rules are duplicated, and a correction may reach only some agents.
I separated reusable knowledge into the ontology and wiki, then selected only the parts needed for each execution. The goal was to make an agent’s knowledge and action boundary inspectable outside its prompt and let several agents share the same knowledge contract.
Representative user scene Consider a request to identify likely causes of repeated equipment stops and propose an inspection sequence.
Classify the equipment, symptom, related process, and expected output in the request. Find connected equipment, parts, failure modes, and inspection documents in the ontology. Retrieve the sequence, allowed tools, sources, and restrictions from the LLM wiki. Compose the analysis agent’s role, inputs, tools, output format, and stop conditions. Run the agent within the allowed data and tool boundary while recording its evidence and result. If the task would change an external system, check the human approval scope, allow or stop the action, and read back the actual result after execution. This is a generalized public description of the implemented direction. It excludes company documents, equipment addresses, accounts, and private operating rules.
A system map for first-time readers This platform is not a single chatbot screen. It has an entry point for the request, an ontology and wiki that supply relevant knowledge, a composition stage that assembles a task-specific agent, a bounded execution stage, and a final evidence and result check.
Five stages of the AI agent platformThe ontology and LLM wiki supply the agent's knowledge and operating rules. Authority and evidence checks remain separate before and after execution. Because there is no public operating UI at this stage, this diagram shows the relationship among the locally validated components.
Generalized from the locally validated foundation·31 Jul 2026
A first-time reader can follow the diagram from left to right. The first three stages decide what agent should be composed. The last two decide what that agent may actually do and whether the observed result matches the request. Answer quality and permission to change an external system therefore remain separate concerns.
Components and responsibilities Component Responsibility Ontology Connect domain concepts and relationships so agents resolve the same objects consistently LLM wiki Provide task guidance, tool instructions, examples, constraints, and validation criteria Agent Composer Turn a request into an executable definition of role, tools, evidence, output, and stop conditions Agent Runner Execute the definition within its allowed boundary and record the process and result Authority & Evidence Layer Check evidence, target identity, and human approval; stop when information is missing and read back the result after execution This separation means a knowledge change can be made in the ontology or wiki instead of editing every agent prompt. The runner records which knowledge was used, while the safety layer keeps analytical success separate from execution authority.
Source structure and reading order The actual repository is not public. The names below are generalized responsibility units for explaining the codebase; they are not copies of private directory names.
knowledge/ ├── ontology/ relationships among equipment, process, documents, and roles └── wiki/ task sequences, tool guidance, and cautions schemas/ agent execution and evidence contracts composer/ selects knowledge and assembles an agent definition runner/ invokes permitted tools and records the run authority/ checks target, human approval, and external-effect scope evidence/ preserves sources, artifact identity, and observed results tests/ exercises stop conditions, replay, and artifact consistency For a first code read, start with knowledge/ to see what an agent can know. Continue through schemas/ and composer/ to see how that knowledge becomes an executable definition. Then read runner/ and authority/ for the action boundary, followed by evidence/ and tests/ for result verification.
Data, AI, and human roles The ontology and wiki retain concepts, relationships, task guidance, sources, scope, and constraints. An agent run records the request, selected knowledge, tools, result, risk, and approval boundary separately. This makes it possible to inspect how an agent was composed and which material it used.
AI assists with request classification, candidate knowledge retrieval, agent-definition drafts, test and counterexample creation, and result summaries. A person reviews the ontology and wiki, chooses the permitted tools and data scope, and approves any external change. A better answer does not transfer human authority to the agent.
Implemented and verified scope In the last completed local snapshot, Python 3.12 and jsonschema were used to validate agent execution definitions, evidence and target bindings, and stop conditions.
150 local regression checks passed Primary and reproduced artifacts rebuilt from source were byte-identical One Windows symlink capability limitation remained recorded as a skip No orders were submitted and no external systems were changed No human operational approval or production connection exists This verifies a local foundation and safety layer for composing and running agents. It does not mean that a public service, live trading, or external-system automation is operational.
Potential company use A company could compose maintenance, process-diagnostic, quality-investigation, or work-standard search agents that use the same internal terms and rules. Knowledge remains in the ontology and wiki, while each agent receives only the role and tools required for its task, reducing duplicated knowledge and prompt variation.
The platform can also retain which knowledge and documents were used, who approved an external change, and what the external system reported afterward. Actual benefit would still need to be measured through company-data integration, user validation, and operating-environment tests.

Real operation still requires quality review of the company ontology and wiki, document-level access control, bounded agent tools, human approval, duplicate-execution protection, and read-back from the external system. Why the shop-floor decision mattered Deep-learning code can run once and still be unusable for an engineering decision if no one can explain which data and settings produced the result. A score can be overstated when samples from the same product or Lot cross training and test boundaries, or when the test set is repeatedly used to guide model changes.
In manufacturing, that problem affects quality decisions directly. Missed defects and false rejections have different costs, and offline behavior can change with equipment, material, or capture conditions. The project therefore starts with a traceable experiment standard rather than a peak score.
Why a digital method was needed A single notebook is useful for fast exploration, but hidden state and cell order can make a result fragile. Separating preprocessing, training, evaluation, and run records makes it possible to trace which change affected the outcome.
MLOps in this case does not mean that a deployment platform has already been built. It means connecting the data identifier, split rule, configuration, code, runtime environment, and evaluation output as one experiment record.
My actual role As a personal learning project, I organized preprocessing, model architecture, evaluation, and system design into topic-based documents, then connected them to a PyTorch training template and a manufacturing-defect example. The repository aims for a path from data splitting and preprocessing through training, evaluation, and reproducibility, but the current public code implements only part of that path as a learning scaffold.
It therefore does not claim a specific dataset size, model accuracy, reproduced training result, or production deployment. Model, industry-case, and performance statements in the study documents are kept separate from repository achievements unless a corresponding run is publicly evidenced.

No separate public web app was visible. The visitor-facing outputs are Markdown tables, Mermaid diagrams, pseudocode, and the three Python sources rather than application screens.

Preprocessing parameters are fitted only on training data and then applied to validation and test data. Final evaluation uses a fixed test set that was not used for model selection, and retains per-class metrics and representative errors rather than only an average score.

Data rights, model version, decision threshold, approval, and rollback also need operating controls.
Under those conditions, a company could review where a model is trustworthy instead of relying on one score. The first minute This case is a training-team Vision AI PoC that classifies weld images into normal and defect candidates. It was not a system that replaced inspectors or made shipment decisions. The team evaluated whether a model could narrow the images that an inspector should review first.
Item What to know Problem The risk of missing small weld defects when normal images dominate the data Team output Public/field data separation, staged model experiments, a second test, and a result report My scope Data-purpose separation, metric and comparison design, and recall-first threshold review Current stage Training PoC evaluation complete; not production-deployed Public screen No runnable inspection screen or report capture is available; only the shareable decision flow is explained The 30-second summary at the top shows the outcome and role boundary first. The main text explains why recall came first, how data moved through the PoC, and how the team result differs from my contribution. The expandable Design and validation record below is the supporting requirements and task appendix.
Why weld-defect detection matters A missed micro-crack or pinhole can allow a defective weld to continue downstream. Flagging a normal part as a defect candidate creates reinspection work. Both have a cost, but this project gave priority to reducing the error that passes a defect as normal.
When normal images greatly outnumber defect images, a model can report high accuracy by predicting normal most of the time. The evaluation therefore did not stop at “How many images were correct?” It considered recall—the share of actual defects found—together with precision, which helps describe the reinspection load.
My battery-cell assembly experience with ultrasonic and laser welding informed that priority. The field experience and the education-project metrics remain separate, however. This case evaluates inspection-assistance potential on bounded material; it does not claim completed autonomous inspection.

It does not mean that the team implemented an operating production system in which a line camera streamed images to a real-time model.
Component Responsibility Not established at this stage Public data Provide broad learning coverage for weld-defect features Prove field performance Field images Check model response under limited capture conditions Represent every machine and product condition Team model experiments Compare stages from DenseNet to ResNet+DeiT Select an operating model from model name alone Threshold evaluation Compare where a defect probability becomes a review candidate Fix one value for every future condition Inspection-assistance rule Send higher-risk candidates to human reinspection Make shipment decisions without a person Error review Return FP and FN cases to data and capture review Assume every error has one model-only cause How data, models, and evaluation connect 1. Separate the purpose of each data source Approximately 60,000 AI-Hub public welding images supplied broad learning coverage. 198 field-practice images provided a separate, limited check under field capture conditions. The two sources were not presented as one undifferentiated set of 60,198 training images. Cameras, illumination, surface reflections, and product conditions differed. Strong results on public data were not treated as proof of the same behavior in the field.
2. Check labels and splits The workflow aligned the meaning of public labels with the field defect definition and kept the same image from appearing in both learning and evaluation. If that boundary fails, a high score may only show that the model saw the same image again.
3. Compare the team’s model stages on one basis The team experiment record progressed from a DenseNet-stage baseline through a two-model combination to a ResNet+DeiT ensemble. The stages were compared under the same F1, recall, and precision frame instead of changing the success rule for each model. I do not present all of that model development as solo work.
4. Turn probabilities into an inspection rule The model outputs a defect probability for each image. A threshold decides when that probability becomes a defect candidate. Lowering the threshold can catch more defects, but it can also send more normal images to reinspection.
Term Plain meaning Why it mattered here Recall The share of actual defects the model found Reduce missed defects first Precision The share of defect candidates that were actual defects Understand the reinspection load F1 A balance between recall and precision Avoid choosing from one favorable metric False negative A defect predicted as normal The error reduced first False positive A normal image predicted as a defect candidate The error connected to reinspection cost 5. Look back at the images behind the metrics The second test reviewed the region where normal and defect predictions mixed. The evaluation first found thresholds that retained 100% recall, compared precision and F1 within that region, and then reviewed FP and FN images to identify the next questions for data, labels, and capture conditions.
Team result versus my contribution Scope Attribution Public and field data preparation, model training and candidate progression, second test, and PoC report Training-team result Separating the intended use of public data and field images My role Organizing a common F1, recall, and precision comparison My role Reviewing recall-first thresholds and interpreting FP and FN behavior My role A claim that I built every model alone, a real-time inspection screen, or production deployment Not claimed as my work In an interview, I explain the complete flow and the work I actually performed. This keeps the team’s models and report as team output while making my evaluation and operating-threshold contribution concrete.
Problems and decisions Problem Decision Reason Normal images can make accuracy hide missed-defect risk Use recall first and inspect precision and F1 with it Separate defect-pass risk from reinspection cost Public and field images have different capture conditions Keep their purposes separate Avoid presenting public-data results as field performance One model behaves differently at different thresholds Compare precision and F1 inside the 100%-recall region Evaluate model choice and inspection policy together Metrics alone do not reveal why errors happened Review the confusion matrix and FP/FN images Return findings to data, label, and capture review Field material and the report cannot be published as-is Publish only a verified text structure Avoid fabricated screens or images with unclear rights Verified result and potential benefits At the selected threshold on the recorded evaluation set, the report lists F1 93.10%, Recall 100%, and Precision 87.07%. Recall 100% means that no defect in that evaluation set was missed. It does not guarantee every future defect or every equipment condition. Precision 87.07% shows that some defect candidates may be normal and require reinspection.
The benefit demonstrated by the PoC was not one metric in isolation. It was a way to turn quality risk into an inspection policy:
a review priority that puts higher-cost candidates in front of an inspector first; one evaluation frame for comparing model candidates; a shared language that links missed defects to quality risk and false alarms to reinspection; and a sequence for returning recurring error images to data and capture improvement. A reduction in escaped defects or inspection time was not measured. Such effects require a controlled comparison before and after production introduction.
Current limitations and next validation The current stage is a bounded PoC. The 198 field images do not cover every equipment, material, lighting, and product-shape condition. Real-time camera input, inference at line speed, dropped frames, long-term performance change, and the operator reinspection procedure were not validated.
Field use would require the following checks:
Build an independent evaluation set split by product or lot. Reconfirm class-level sample counts and label rules with quality specialists. Standardize camera position, illumination, focus, and capture timing. Test inference latency and dropped frames at line speed. Trace model version, threshold, image, equipment condition, and reinspection result together. Provide change approval and a path back to an earlier model and threshold. Field images and company quality criteria are also not disclosed. The page therefore does not substitute another project’s screen or a third-party welding image.

The flow below generalizes the team exercise for a virtual-commissioning context.
The first minute In this case, “Giga Press” names a training scenario in which a factory adds another process cell around a large casting machine. Instead of waiting for the equipment to arrive before aligning PLC sequences, screen tags, and upstream data, the team connected them around a virtual machine and repeated failure cases first.
Item What to know Team output A demonstration and report connecting a Factory I/O virtual machine, PLC, SCADA, and an OPC UA flow Project form A ten-person education team PoC, not the construction of a production Giga Press My scope AI-model candidate selection and training, communications setup including OPC UA, and technical research Teammates’ scope PLC Ladder logic and SCADA screen and tag implementation Current evidence Team demonstration and report stage; no live-plant HIL, FAT, or before-and-after result measurement The factory-expansion scenario The team assumed that a factory was adding a cell similar to an existing process. Copying the machine is not enough. The teams also need to agree on the sensor sequence, when the previous process sends completion, which alarms the operator sees, and whether upstream systems understand equipment state under the same names.
If that work starts only on the physical machine, missing sensors, delayed completion signals, manual/automatic mode conflicts, and restart conditions may appear late. This PoC used Factory I/O in place of the machine while connecting the PLC sequence, SCADA display, and OPC UA data flow. It reviewed stop and recovery conditions as well as the normal run.
Complete system architecture flowchart LR A["Factory I/Ovirtual sensors, actuators, and process motion"] <-->|"I/O signals"| B["PLC and Laddersequence, interlocks, and final run permission"] B <-->|"state, alarms, and manual-action results"| C["SCADAoperator screens and alarms"] B -->|"equipment tags"| D["OPC UA boundaryvalue, quality, and time"] D --> E["Web status-view candidate"] D --> F["DQN optimization candidateadvisory review"] G["Future physical sensors and actuators"] -. "replace the virtual machineduring HIL and FAT" .-> A Each component had a distinct responsibility.
Component Responsibility Not its responsibility Factory I/O Run a virtual process with sensors and actuators and repeat fault conditions Prove hydraulic, servo, or safety behavior of the physical machine PLC and Ladder Decide process sequence, interlocks, and final run permission Execute an AI output without review SCADA Display state, alarms, and operator-action results Replace the safety circuit or PLC interlocks OPC UA Carry PLC data to upper layers as tags Guarantee a value is safe merely because communication succeeded Web and AI candidates Display state or examine optimization potential Own emergency stop or machine authority The Ladder and SCADA implementations belonged to the responsible teammates. I do not present this architecture as a solo build. My work was to review and train the DQN candidate, set up the communications path including OPC UA, and research how the components should meet at their boundaries.
How one signal moves Consider a virtual “die ready” signal.
A virtual sensor in Factory I/O creates the ready state. The PLC checks the current mode, completion of the preceding step, and related interlocks. If the conditions agree, the PLC permits the next action. If they do not, it keeps the process stopped with a cause. SCADA presents the same state as an equipment name and alarm an operator can understand. OPC UA carries equipment, signal, value, quality, and time information to upper layers. A web view or AI candidate consumes that data, but it does not bypass the PLC safety decision to move equipment. The team design treated matching signal names as insufficient. equipment, signal, value, quality, and timestamp were needed together so a stale value after communications loss would not look like a current healthy state. The actual tag list and equipment addresses remain in internal team material and are not reproduced here.
My model and communications work DQN candidate selection and training I selected and trained a DQN candidate to examine whether real-time sensor and PLC states could support process optimization. The important questions were not the model name alone:
Which PLC and sensor states should become observations? How should a reward distinguish shorter cycle behavior from safety violations? Where should an AI output remain advisory so it cannot bypass PLC interlocks? The project has no repeated production-machine measurement of model performance or operating benefit. The DQN is therefore described as an upper-layer optimization candidate, not a production controller.
OPC UA setup and technical research I organized where the OPC UA connection belonged so PLC values could retain a common meaning across SCADA, web, and AI layers. The setup considered the meaning of a tag, communication quality, and time rather than transferring addresses alone. I also researched why loss of communication, stale values, and state synchronization after reconnect should be separate test cases, then reflected those concerns in the team scenario.
Ten-person team result versus my role Scope Attribution Process scenario, the complete Factory I/O–PLC–SCADA–OPC UA connection, integrated demo, and report Ten-person team result AI-model candidate selection and training, communications setup, and related technical research My role PLC Ladder sequences and interlock implementation Responsible teammate’s role SCADA screens, tags, and alarm implementation Responsible teammate’s role This distinction is more than an R&R table. In an interview, it lets me explain the complete system context while keeping the work I did not implement—Ladder and SCADA—out of my individual contribution.
Work sequence Define the expansion case. The team mapped the normal sequence plus stop, delay, missing-sensor, manual/automatic mode, and restart conditions. Assign signal responsibility. It separated PLC decisions, SCADA display, and data sent to upper layers. Connect virtual process and control. The responsible teammate connected Factory I/O scenarios to Ladder logic. Build the operator view. The responsible teammate configured SCADA state, alarms, and action results on the same signal basis. Review AI and communications candidates. I selected and trained the DQN candidate, set up the OPC UA flow, and researched the supporting design. Integrate normal, failure, and recovery flows. The team combined the parts into one demonstration and report. Review claim boundaries. The team output, individual contribution, expected effects, and uncompleted plant validation were kept separate. Problems and decisions Problem Decision Reason The virtual machine, PLC, and screen can interpret one signal differently Define a shared tag meaning together with value, quality, and time A screen can look healthy while showing a stale value Failure cases are difficult and risky to repeat on physical equipment Review missing sensors, delay, and restart in Factory I/O first Find logic and display errors before physical trial AI response and networks introduce delay and variability Keep final run permission and interlocks in the PLC An optimization candidate must not replace safety decisions Different people implemented different layers Separate the team result from individual roles in the document Explain the whole context without overstating individual implementation The report included efficiency targets Label targets separately from measured results Prevent expected effects from being mistaken for achieved outcomes Verified result and potential benefits The verified result is the ten-person team demonstration and report connecting the process flow, Factory I/O and Ladder, SCADA, OPC UA, and the placement of web and AI extensions. It showed a method for reviewing sequence, signal names, alarms, and communications failures on one basis before equipment installation.
The report’s 50–75% setup-time reduction and 50% equipment-expansion labor reduction are expected effects or targets for successful virtual commissioning and Ladder modularization. They are not controlled before-and-after plant measurements and are not presented as project achievements.
After a controlled comparison against a plant baseline, potential benefits could include:
finding sequence and tag mismatches before physical equipment trial; reusing signal definitions and failure/recovery test order during expansion; giving controls, operator-interface, communications, and analytics teams a common description of state; and reviewing how a logic change affects other process steps and alarms before commissioning. Current limitations and next validation The PoC was not validated on physical Giga Press hardware, a safety PLC, hydraulic or servo dynamics, live takt conditions, or production I/O. It also did not measure DQN performance in a live plant, long-duration communications stability, or operator response to alarms.
Field use would require hardware-in-the-loop testing with actual I/O, FAT, communications-loss and reconnect tests, tag-version changes, alarm priorities, network segmentation, and access review. Even if an AI candidate is used, it needs accept, reject, and rollback paths for its recommendations. Machine commands and safety decisions must remain with validated PLC and safety systems.

The case explains a general flow from manufacturing terminology contracts to retrieval.
What this project is The same machine or defect can have different names across manufacturing documents. When process instructions, quality criteria, equipment history, and corrective-action records use inconsistent terminology, finding a document does not establish that it refers to the same object.
HeungTology is a personal experiment that stores industrial-knowledge documents as Markdown nodes and indexes their YAML front matter and body text in a local vector store. It is a Git repository containing a knowledge collection and a local Python CLI, not a public web service or graph dashboard.

Public GitHub repository·31 Jul 2026

The local flow visible in code is prepare Markdown nodes → run --sync to read front matter and body text → create BGE-M3 embeddings → upsert into ChromaDB → enter a query → retrieve candidates → rerank with BGE reranker → apply time decay and hash status → print a terminal scoreboard. The current CLI prints candidate filenames, parent information, and scores. It does not provide a web page or a natural-language answer screen.
Data flow and component responsibilities Component Responsibility 02_Knowledge/ Store domain Markdown bodies and YAML front matter rag_cli_v2.py Walk and parse documents, synchronize ChromaDB, run vector retrieval and reranking, apply time decay and a limited hash comparison, and print terminal output 02_Knowledge/_System/ Store the ontology map and large index artifacts included in the public repository README.md Explain project intent and example commands; it is not a substitute for tests or reproducible evidence The public CLI does not connect to Neo4j or generate JSON-LD, OWL, or SHACL files. Those terms remain in repository design language, but this case does not present them as behavior executed by the current public code.
Public repository structure and reading order HeungTology/ ├─ README.md ├─ rag_cli_v2.py └─ 02_Knowledge/ ├─ [MOC] 00_INDEX.md ├─ _System/ │ ├─ _Ontology_Map.json │ └─ _index/ ├─ 01_Semiconductor/ ├─ 02_Battery/ ├─ 03_AI_Data/ └─ ...domain knowledge folders Recommended order: ① use the README for a short statement of intent, ② read rag_cli_v2.py for the actual synchronization and query path, ③ inspect [MOC] 00_INDEX.md and one Concept or Data document to see the front-matter and body format, and ④ examine _Ontology_Map.json and _index artifacts last. Large index files and self-reported figures inside documents are not achievement evidence unless their generation and evaluation can also be reproduced.
My actual role As a personal project, I structured metadata for Markdown knowledge nodes and implemented the local retrieval flow in rag_cli_v2.py. The script maps domain, object type, parent relationship, tier, date, and trust fields into search metadata, reranks retrieved candidates, and applies time decay and a hash-comparison result to the score.
What is implemented and what remains limited The public code supports Markdown front-matter parsing, ChromaDB synchronization, BGE-M3 embedding retrieval, BGE reranking, date-based score decay, a limited evidence_hash comparison, and a terminal scoreboard.
The repository does not currently include a dependency manifest, automated tests, portable path and device settings, a web UI, or a public runtime URL. The CLI assumes Windows absolute paths, local CUDA, and pre-existing model and database resources, so it is not presented as a reproducible clean-checkout application. Several repository documents also retain pending_review, placeholder, and [데이터 부재] markers; performance figures and completion declarations inside those documents are not treated as verified results.
This case therefore claims no node count, accuracy, latency, error or warning count, or release grade. Accuracy, authorization, and freshness for real company-document retrieval require separate data and an operating environment.
Conditions for company use Company use would require named terminology owners, controlled change and review procedures, source-acceptance rules, access control, and audit history. Retrieval must remain read-only and separate from equipment control so unsupported text cannot become an operating condition or work instruction.
With those controls and a reproducible installation and evaluation path, common metadata and relationships could help teams find process conditions, equipment history, and corrective-action evidence across departmental vocabulary. The current public result is not that operating outcome; it is a reviewable starting point for the document structure and local retrieval experiment.

The case is described as a generalized robot data flow separating control authority from observation.
